title: Not all at once
objective: Lower blood pressure in a hypertensive emergency gradually with titrated IV agents under close monitoring, because an abrupt fall can injure the organs at risk

brief.situation: 21:00 on a progressive care unit. Mrs. Mensah, 54, came up from the emergency department with a blood pressure of 228/132, a pounding headache and blurred vision. She ran out of her blood pressure tablets two weeks ago.
handover: CT head in the department: no bleed. Creatinine up from her baseline. No chest or back pain; pulses equal in both arms.

The provider's order: the titratable IV antihypertensive infusion, titrated to lower the mean arterial pressure by no more than 25% in the first hour, then toward 160/100 over the next 2 to 6 hours; blood pressure every 5 minutes; neurological checks every 15 minutes; call for any new neurological sign or chest pain.
The provider is on the unit.
howItWorks: The clock runs in simulated time; study pace runs three simulated minutes per real minute. Pause any time.
Assess and act as you think the patient needs. Each assessment takes the time on its button.
Partway through you are asked to write what you think is happening. A debrief scores what you did.

source.note: Encephalopathy and kidney injury advance at this pressure. FLAG. Simplified teaching model written for exam practice; not a validated physiological model. Disease courses, effect sizes and local waits are authored and carry FLAG.

Titration slows the injury; the brain still swells for a while. FLAG. Simplified teaching model written for exam practice; not a validated physiological model. Disease courses, effect sizes and local waits are authored and carry FLAG.

The authored point of new confusion and vomiting: worsening hypertensive encephalopathy. FLAG. Simplified teaching model written for exam practice; not a validated physiological model. Disease courses, effect sizes and local waits are authored and carry FLAG.

The authored point of a seizure or a bleed. FLAG. Simplified teaching model written for exam practice; not a validated physiological model. Disease courses, effect sizes and local waits are authored and carry FLAG.
The provider called within 5 minutes of a new neurological sign (the order).
The titrated infusion started within 5 minutes of arrival, with checks every 5 minutes (the order).
A focused assessment or question: about 1 min.
About 10 minutes for the provider to reassess and move her to intensive care; a routine plan about 10 minutes.

why.question: Mrs. Mensah is confused and vomiting while the infusion runs. What is happening, and what do you do?

parts.label: What is happening
parts.criteria: A hypertensive emergency with encephalopathy (confusion, vomiting, worse headache) and kidney injury; lowering too fast risks brain underperfusion, so the goal is no more than 25% in the first hour.
parts.modelAnswer: This is a hypertensive emergency and her encephalopathy is getting worse: confusion, vomiting, worse headache. The pressure must come down, but slowly: no more than 25% in the first hour, or her brain is underperfused.

parts.label: What I do
parts.criteria: Provider now; continue titration to the order's goal (no extra pushes); neuro checks; arterial line; hand off.
parts.modelAnswer: Call the provider now, keep titrating to the order's goal without extra pushes, keep neuro checks and the arterial line going, and hand off.

noProgress.rationale: A hypertensive emergency still uncontrolled with encephalopathy an hour on is harm here.

unsafe.headline: Pushed to normal
unsafe.body: In a hypertensive emergency the pressure comes down gradually: about 25% in the first hour, then toward 160/100 over 2 to 6 hours. Faster risks a stroke.

worsened.headline: Seizure
worsened.body: Encephalopathy can progress to seizures. Start the titrated drug at once and call any new neurological sign.

wrongRoute.headline: Left until the next check
wrongRoute.body: New confusion during a hypertensive emergency needs the provider now.

target.headline: Gradual and escalated
target.body: Titrated by the order, monitored closely, and the change called within minutes. That is the expert path.

recovered.headline: Intensive care, with delays
recovered.body: Check when the infusion started and how long the confusion went before the call.

time_up.headline: Still in crisis
time_up.body: Hypertensive emergency needs titrated treatment within minutes.

scoring.modelReasoning: A pressure of 228/132 with headache, blurred vision and kidney injury is a hypertensive emergency. The titratable IV drug starts at once, lowering the pressure by no more than 25% in the first hour, with checks every 5 minutes and an arterial line. New confusion and vomiting are worsening encephalopathy: the provider comes now. Pushing to normal would starve the brain.

whyQ.ask: While the team takes over: why not lower it faster?
whyQ.explain: The blood pressure should be lowered gradually to prevent brain dysfunction from low perfusion.
